findings.text: The opening paragraph tells a newcomer clearly what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, all in a few sentences. This is the page's strongest part.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The second section, near the top of the page, is an error message instead of the promised proof. The opening promises models, a checker's verdict and costs, but a newcomer never sees any of them, so the case for why Athena matters goes unshown.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: This link sits in the header and talks to an owner, not a visitor. A newcomer can't tell whether it is meant for them or what the "proposals" are.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and in order: prerequisites, clone, setup.sh, then a first command, with a note on what happens when you press Enter. A newcomer knows what to do next. The page does say Athena records what each step cost. But it never says that running it uses paid model calls or needs a Claude account, so a newcomer can't tell what a first run will cost them.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" / "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state machine of firstmate, a different project, full of exit codes and claim ids. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to work out alone that this is a sample of Athena's output, not material they must understand.
findings.source: Heading "Transitions" and cards t1–t12; "the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued"

findings.text: Several glossary entries say the term is undefined. That is honest, and it shows the page traces every statement to a source, but it leaves a first-time reader with terms they still can't pin down.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." / "The firstmate source does not define an endpoint."

findings.text: The page explains its citation scheme up front, and every claim links to exact lines at a fixed commit. This shows a newcomer what "traceable" means in practice, even though the real-job proof is missing.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."
